transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-22 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~52 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Strata - Head of ML), Noah Patel (Strata - SRE), Evelyn Brooks (Strata - CTO)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on latency and throughput targets for both hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment. Customer wants p95 goals, concurrency expectations, streaming behavior, and a token/sec benchmarking plan. Discussed fallbacks, quantization and KV/prefix caching. Agreed next steps for benchmarks and docs.

Topics: p95 targets; concurrency and QPS; streaming to client; token/sec benchmarking; Dedicated node sizing; security (SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS); rollout/POC schedule.

00:00:12 Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we're gonna kick off, we're Maya and Diego from Redwood, and then i think we have Laura, Noah and Evelyn from Strata, is that right?
00:00:20 Laura Kim: yep that's right, thanks Maya, appreciate it.
00:00:23 Diego Ruiz: quick agenda, latencies you care about, concurrency and throughput, streaming/early-token behavior, and then a proposed benchmark/POC plan. sound good?
00:00:31 Evelyn Brooks: sounds good to me.
00:00:33 Noah Patel: yep fine.
00:00:36 Maya Chen: cool, Laura—maybe you can share the current production numbers and what your success criteria look like?
00:00:42 Laura Kim: yeah, so at a high level we run a customer-facing chat assistant and also a batch summarization job. For chat we need p95 under 350ms ideally for short interactions (<256 tokens), p99 is less strict but we'd like decent tail, and we need streaming for tokens as they arrive. Concurrency for chat is tricky — on busy days we hit sustained 150 concurrent chat sessions and bursts up to 500, but those are short. For summarization we do large generations, 512-1024 tokens, throughput matters more than p95, we target about 40-60 reqs per second for batch pipelines.
00:01:35 Maya Chen: ok that's helpful — when you say p95 under 350ms are you measuring from first byte to last token or e2e including network to client?
00:01:44 Laura Kim: that's server-side generation latency, so last token emitted server-side. We measure end-to-end client as well but server-side is the primary SLO.
00:01:52 Diego Ruiz: got it. For streaming, are you expecting early token delivery latency to be the same p95 target or do you accept lower guarantees for first-byte?
00:02:02 Laura Kim: First-byte we'd like under 100-150ms p95 if possible, because we show typing indicators and it needs to feel instant.
00:02:11 Noah Patel: and to add — we run across aws eu and us regions, we care about multi-region fallbacks. Also security: SOC2 and SAML, and we use KMS to manage keys.
00:02:24 Maya Chen: totally, we support SAML SSO and integrations with KMS/HSM for Private deployments; for Hosted we have encryption at rest and key handling—we'll share the security pack.
00:02:33 Evelyn Brooks: good. ok can you explain how Dedicated differs for latency? like what guarantees we get vs Hosted?
00:02:40 Diego Ruiz: yeah so Dedicated is reserved GPU pools—predictable throughput and isolation. For strict p95 numbers we recommend Dedicated because autoscaling in Hosted can add variability during bursts. Also Dedicated lets you pick instance types, control quantization, and maintain warmed KV cache which reduces tail for repeated prefixes.
00:02:58 Laura Kim: when you say warmed KV cache, can you explain? we've got a lot of identical prefixes for our product FAQs.
00:03:05 Diego Ruiz: sure — during serving we maintain a KV cache for the model key-value states so if many requests reuse the prefix, we can avoid recomputing early layers. that effectively turns some of your work into cached ops, dropping token/sec compute and improving p95. sometimes the transcript system writes it as K-V cash, but it's KV cache.
00:03:23 Noah Patel: interesting, do you do cross-request prefix reuse automatically? we have slightly different user contexts so maybe partial reuse.
00:03:31 Diego Ruiz: we do prefix caching heuristics — you can configure TTL and matching thresholds. for partial overlap we still get benefits from shared KV keys if the initial tokens match.
00:03:39 Maya Chen: quick question on models — what model families are you evaluating, do you plan to use open weights or a hosted model?
00:03:46 Laura Kim: we're looking at open families, a Mistral-ish medium sized model for chat, and for summarization a larger 30B variant. cost is a concern so quantization would help.
00:03:55 Diego Ruiz: great, we typically recommend 16-bit for quality-critical flows then 8-bit/quantized 4-bit for heavy throughput where you can accept small quality deltas. we also expose model variants on the same API so fallbacks are straightforward.
00:04:08 Laura Kim: and how do you measure token/sec in the benchmark? we have mixed prompt lengths.
00:04:13 Diego Ruiz: our bench plan will run three mixes: short 32 tokens, mid 256 tokens, long 1024 tokens. for each we measure throughput (requests/sec), tokens/sec, and p50/p95/p99 generation latency, both for cold and warmed KV cache scenarios. we'll run at target concurrencies you give us and then ramp to find tail behavior.
00:04:33 Maya Chen: and we can stream tokens to you so you can measure first-byte latency accurately.
00:04:36 Laura Kim: okay nice.
00:04:39 Noah Patel: what's your continuous batching behavior? we worry that batching to improve token/sec hurts first-byte latency for short chats.
00:04:47 Diego Ruiz: good point — our runtime supports dynamic batching with latency SLOs; requests that need low first-byte can be prioritized into smaller batches or even singleton paths. we also do workload-aware batching, so long-running batch jobs are scheduled separately from low-latency paths. you can tune this by route.
00:05:03 Evelyn Brooks: so we'd be able to pin chat to a low-latency profile and set summarization to a throughput profile?
00:05:08 Diego Ruiz: exactly. routing policies let you route by latency class, model variant, and region.
00:05:12 Laura Kim: what about concurrency per GPU — we currently see concurrency spikes; how many concurrent streams can a single Dedicated GPU handle for your recommended model?
00:05:21 Diego Ruiz: it depends on model size and quantization. rough numbers: for a 7B quantized model you might get tens to low hundreds of concurrent short-chat sessions per 80GB GPU with streaming; for 30B it's lower, maybe single-digit to low double-digit for strict p95. we'll provide solid numbers in bench.
00:05:40 Maya Chen: we'll include a matrix with tokens/sec and concurrency per instance type in the deliverable.
00:05:44 Laura Kim: good. any suggestions to reduce p95 without huge cost increases?
00:05:48 Diego Ruiz: yes — prefix caching, smaller model variants for chat, streaming first-byte optimizations, and aggressive quantization where quality tolerates it. also using dedicated warmed pools eliminates cold-start and autoscaler jitter.
00:05:59 Noah Patel: for our batch summarization we'd like to know peak tokens/sec for a cluster — like we want to process 1M tokens per minute, how do we translate to nodes?
00:06:10 Diego Ruiz: we'll convert tokens/sec to GPU-hours in the benchmark report; but rule of thumb: measure tokens/sec per GPU for your chosen model/quant, then divide. so if a node does 10k tokens/sec, 1M tokens/min = 16.7k tokens/sec, you'd need ~2 nodes. we'll do concrete tests.
00:06:27 Laura Kim: ok. let's talk SLAs — do you provide latency SLAs on Dedicated?
00:06:32 Maya Chen: Dedicated gives uptime SLAs and predictable throughput targets; latency SLOs are customer-specific and we'll commit in the SOW based on bench results and pinned capacity.
00:06:42 Evelyn Brooks: security again — for Private/on-prem we need KMS and audit logs, can you deliver?
00:06:47 Maya Chen: yes Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit logging with retention options, and can be deployed into customer VPC/on-prem. we'll attach our security pack.
00:06:56 Noah Patel: any concerns about data residency/regulatory compliance? we have EU data residency needs.
00:07:01 Maya Chen: we can run Dedicated in EU regions and support Private for strict residency; we'll highlight region options in the docs.
00:07:07 Laura Kim: love it.
00:07:10 Diego Ruiz: back to bench specifics — can you confirm the concurrency distribution? like what percent of requests are short vs long?
00:07:18 Laura Kim: roughly 80% short chat (avg 48 tokens), 15% mid, 5% long. spikes push short to 95%. bursts come in minute-long windows.
00:07:28 Diego Ruiz: thanks, that's exactly what we need. we'll simulate that mix and run ramp tests to find the p95 cliff.
00:07:34 Maya Chen: any current infra? are you running models yourselves now?
00:07:38 Laura Kim: we've been self-hosting on EC2/GPU with a custom server; but ops burden is high and tail behavior is inconsistent. looking for simpler dev experience and predictability.
00:07:47 Maya Chen: makes sense. Redwood Hosted is fastest to try, but for the strict p95 you'd described Dedicated or Private will probably be the better fit.
00:07:55 Evelyn Brooks: question on fallbacks — if Dedicated hits capacity, what's the fallback?
00:07:59 Diego Ruiz: we route by policy — can fallback to a compatible hosted variant or alternative model with slightly higher latency but lower cost. you can set auto-fallback thresholds.
00:08:09 Noah Patel: do you support per-tenant isolation on Dedicated? some of our data is different for customers.
00:08:14 Maya Chen: Dedicated provides isolation and you can set tenant routing and per-tenant quotas; Private gives even stronger isolation for regulated customers.
00:08:21 Laura Kim: ok great.
00:08:23 Maya Chen: any final open questions before we move to next steps?
00:08:26 Laura Kim: can you outline the bench phases quickly?
00:08:29 Diego Ruiz: sure — Phase 1: baseline on Hosted quick tests, Phase 2: Dedicated sizing tests with your prompt set (short/mid/long mixes) including warmed vs cold cache measurements, Phase 3: longer soak and regional failover tests. we'll produce a results matrix with p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and recommended node counts.
00:08:49 Maya Chen: and we'll include suggested quantization configurations and expected quality tradeoffs.
00:08:54 Laura Kim: perfect. what about duration/cost for the POC?
00:08:58 Maya Chen: typical Dedicated POC is 2-4 weeks depending on scale; we'll include pricing options in the doc.
00:09:05 Evelyn Brooks: sounds reasonable.
00:09:08 Noah Patel: one more — do you expose tracing or per-token cost breakdowns for debugging regressions?
00:09:14 Diego Ruiz: yes Redwood Console surfaces per-route token cost, latency breakdowns, traces, and error analysis; we'll export traces for bench runs and attach them to the report.
00:09:25 Laura Kim: excellent.
00:09:27 Maya Chen: ok, to recap: Laura to send prompt set and concurrency profile by Friday; Diego will prepare bench plan and run initial benchmarks on Dedicated; Maya will send pricing and security docs. We'll schedule a POC kickoff next week.
00:09:40 Laura Kim: yep will do. thanks everyone.
00:09:43 Maya Chen: thanks all.
